big_idea: 100 cm = 1 m. Use BENCHMARKS — fingernail = 1 cm, hockey stick = 1 m.
learning_intention: We are learning to use cm and m and estimate with benchmarks.
student_learning_goal: I can use cm and m and estimate with benchmarks.
success_criteria: I can say that 100 cm = 1 m.
I can use HOCKEY STICK = 1 m.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Roo and Cal — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Roo: STANDARD UNITS! Centimetres are SMALL. Metres are BIG. 100 centimetres = 1 metre! Roo opens with the unit refrain: 'SMALL unit, BIG count — BIG unit, small count!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Yesterday Roo measured with HAND-SPANS — but Aaron's hand-span and Bea's hand-span are different sizes! Today STANDARD units (cm, m) make sure EVERY classroom counts the same way.

Bring children to the carpet. Roo and Cal puppets. 'Friends — yesterday non-standard units. Today STANDARD UNITS: centimetres and metres.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write CENTIMETRE, METRE, BENCHMARK on chart. 'Centimetre (cm) = small unit. Metre (m) = big unit. 100 cm = 1 m.'

Demonstrate. Show a centimetre strip. 'This is 1 cm — about a fingernail width.' Hold fingernail. 'See!'

Show a metre strip. 'This is 1 metre — about a hockey stick.' Compare to a real hockey stick.

'Benchmark = a familiar thing we use to ESTIMATE.'

More benchmarks:
- 1 cm: fingernail width, paperclip width, eraser tip.
- 1 m: hockey stick, doorway height divided by 2, average kid's arm-span.
- 100 cm: half of teacher's height, height of countertop.

Demo conversion. 'A 1 metre strip — how many cm? Count the marks.' Count: 100. '100 cm = 1 m. ALWAYS!'

More practice:
- '50 cm = HALF a metre.'
- '200 cm = 2 metres.'
- '10 cm = 1/10 of a metre.'

'Roo says — use BENCHMARKS to estimate. Then check with a ruler.'

'Today YOU estimate with benchmarks AND check.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: estimate 4 lengths with benchmarks.
Three stations. A: Estimate 5 lengths with benchmarks. B: Convert 5 between cm and m. C: Find an object close to 1 m.
Stretch at C: estimate 5 different lengths in mixed cm/m.
Discuss when to use cm vs m.

STRATEGY COMPARE: Two pairs share HOW they estimated the doorway — whose-arm-span vs hockey-stick-count vs counting tiles. Class debates which is most reliable. Cite Lehrer (2003) — standard units exist BECAUSE non-standard ones can't be shared across classrooms.
steps.teacher_prompt: Roo: 'Different bodies = different counts. STANDARD units fix that.'

differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children find objects ABOUT 1 m and ABOUT 1 cm. NO-PAPER PATH: use FINGERNAIL (~1 cm) and ARM-SPAN (~1 m) on the body. Children compare body benchmarks to objects.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: knows 100 cm = 1 m; uses benchmarks; estimates correctly.

discussion_prompts: How many cm in a metre?
When use cm? When use m?
consolidation.exit_routine: Roo's standard refrain — 'SMALL unit, BIG count — BIG unit, small count!' (3x). Each child writes one classroom object measured in BOTH cm and m on a sticky.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child says 100 cm = 100 m — repairing the same-unit-different-name trap at Grade 2
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On standard units (cm, m), the trap is unit-conversion confusion (Lehrer 2003 measurement units; Sarama & Clements 2009): child treats cm and m as unrelated rather than nested (100 cm = 1 m). Without unit-relation understanding, ruler use (Lesson 3) and tape-measure work cannot ground.

Yesterday Roo measured with hand-spans. Today STANDARD units let EVERY classroom count the same. Lesson 3 ruler use; Lesson 4 time; Lesson 5 capstones.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair at B. Child writes '100 cm = 100 m' for conversion.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Roo asks — is a centimetre the SAME size as a metre?'

Child says no. 'Right! cm is SMALL. m is BIG. 100 cm makes ONE m, not 100 m.'

Demonstrate. Lay out 100 cm strips end-to-end. They reach 1 m. 'See — 100 of these little ones = 1 big one.'

Generlise. 'Roo says — 100 cm is the SAME LENGTH as 1 m. Different names, same length.'

If still confused: provide a side-by-side ruler showing 1 m = 100 cm marks.
common_misconceptions: cm and m are the same. (Repair: different sizes.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child treats cm and m as unrelated: physical demo with metre stick + 100 cubes; child counts 100 cubes ALONG the metre stick.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child uses cm where m is appropriate (e.g., doorway height in cm): drill 'big object → big unit; small object → small unit.'
DIAGNOSTIC C — child knows units but converts wrong: drill 100 cm = 1 m as a benchmark; child re-states before any conversion.

parts_outline.task: Estimate 5 lengths in cm OR m using benchmarks.
Convert 5 measurements between cm and m.
Find 3 objects at home: 1 about 1 cm, 1 about 1 m, 1 about 50 cm.
